newsitem.title: USA: NHL-RED WINGS CAPITALIZE ON FLYERS' MISTAKES.
newsitem.headline: NHL-RED WINGS CAPITALIZE ON FLYERS' MISTAKES.

text.p: They say defence is what wins the Stanley Cup. Bad defence can lose it.
The Detroit Red Wings capitalised on a bounty of defensive mistakes by the Philadelphia Flyers to win the first game of the best-of-seven National Hockey League Stanley Cup Finals 4-2 Saturday night.
The Wings, using their signature graceful, fluid skating, filled every space of open ice in Game 1, and when the puck was coughed up, when mistakes were made, they were there.
Detroit's victory was a clinic in how to play a game in which the object is to allow your opponents to beat themselves.

The Red Wings were there, only six minutes after the start of the game -- seconds after their own right wing Tomas Sandstrom was penalised for high-sticking -- when the Flyers defencemen got caught playing too deep in Detroit's end of the ice.

The puck bounced free, as it often does, but there was no one home at the Flyers' end. Detroit's Kirk Maltby, flying in against Flyers goaltender Ron Hextall with centre Kris Draper and no Flyer in sight, had a short-handed goal while some Philadelphia fans were still finding their seats.
Philadelphia tied the score only 59 seconds when centre Rod Brind'Amour, lingering in front of Detroit goaltender Mike Vernon, stuffed the puck through a scrum of players.

The Red Wings were there again with about four minutes left in the first period when Philadelphia defenceman Kjell Samuelsson, who had been sidelined since January after having surgery to his back, made a blind pass that landed directly on the stick of Detroit wing Joe Kocur.
Again, there was nothing but open ice all the way to the Flyers' net.
"We did make some bad decisions," Flyers' captain Eric Lindros said solemnly after the game.

Every time the Flyers seemed to get their legs back under them and start to dictate the flow of play -- which is critical if their style of bruising body checking is to be successful - they made another mistake, and the Red Wings were there.
Detroit seemed to arrive with the game that Philadelphia was hoping to play. Detroit didn't suffer a lot of body checks. They gave them.
Detroit controlled the middle of the ice, and controlled the areas in front of the goaltenders, something for which the Flyers are known.

With about 12 minutes left in the second period, a face-off in Detroit's defensive zone turned into fierce shooting by the Flyers. And then it turned into a loose puck. Then it turned into yet another Detroit breakaway, this time by centre Sergei Fedorov.
With a slapshot blast, it was 3-1 Detroit, and the game was in their control.

"I don't think that the (Red Wings') speed was an area that I am concerned about at all," Flyers coach Terry Murray said. "What I was concerned about here after this game tonight is the way we played as a team. That's as poorly as we've played in a month and a half."

The Flyers' defencemen were shaky. They made hasty passes into wide open areas, a deadly play when the other team skates so well. They hesitated at key times. In the three previous series leading up to the finals, the Flyers never had to worry about being the first to the puck. They do now.
"I thought that the checking game would be a big part of our game going into tonight. It ended up being a very small part of it because of our neutral zone decisions," Murray said.
After the game, Russian sharpshooter Federov was asked how the Red Wings would approach Game 2. "We will try to play a tight checking and defensive game," he said.
They say defence wins the Stanley Cup.
